lead: Union, concatenation, star, reversal and homomorphism keep a language context-free, and so does intersecting it with a regular set; intersection of two context-free languages and complement do not. These closure properties let you reason about whole families without rebuilding grammars: to show a language is context-free you assemble it from known pieces, and to show it is not you intersect with a regular set and land on a language the pumping lemma kills. Compiler front ends use the same split: a regular lexer feeding a context-free parser.
prereq: You need: 3.1 for grammar notation, Unit 1 for DFA, and Unit 2 for closure of regular languages.

blocks.text: A closure property says: apply the operation to context-free languages and the result is again context-free. The proof is a construction: write the two grammars, add one new start symbol, and show the new grammar generates exactly the intended set.

items: Union: from G1 = (V1, Σ, R1, S1) and G2 = (V2, Σ, R2, S2), take variables V1 ∪ V2 ∪ {S} and rules R1 ∪ R2 ∪ {S → S1, S → S2}. The first step chooses a branch, so the language is L1 ∪ L2.
Concatenation: the same variables with one new rule S → S1S2. A derivation is a derivation in G1 then one in G2, so the language is L1L2.
Kleene star: new rules S → SS1 and S → ε. The recursion adds any number of copies of L1, including none.
Reversal: reverse the right side of every rule, so A → α becomes A → αᴿ. The grammar generates L1ᴿ.
Homomorphism: replace each terminal a everywhere by h(a). If h(a) = ε you create ε-rules, which a CFG allows.

blocks.text: Before combining, rename variables so V1 and V2 are disjoint. Otherwise a rule of G1 can fire inside a derivation of G2, and the grammar generates strings in neither language.
If L is context-free and R is regular, then L ∩ R is context-free. Only one side may be regular.

Take a PDA M for L and a DFA D for R. Build the product machine: a state is a pair (p, q), p a state of M and q a state of D. Each input symbol moves both parts at once, M changing state and stack, D changing state. Accept when both accept. The product accepts exactly L ∩ R.

Grammar version: variables are triples [A, p, q], read as “A derives every string that drives D from p to q”. A rule A → a becomes [A, p, q] → a for each q with δ(p, a) = q. A rule A → BC becomes [A, p, q] → [B, p, r][C, r, q] for every state r.
Use it to prove non-context-freeness: if L ∩ R is not context-free and R is regular, then L is not context-free.

sections.h3: Not closed under intersection or complement

blocks.text: Let L1 = {aⁿbⁿcᵐ : n, m ≥ 0} with grammar S1 → AC, A → aAb | ε, C → cC | ε. Let L2 = {aᵐbⁿcⁿ : n, m ≥ 0} with grammar S2 → DB, D → aD | ε, B → bBc | ε. Both are context-free.
A string in both has as many a's as b's (L1) and as many b's as c's (L2). So L1 ∩ L2 = {aⁿbⁿcⁿ : n ≥ 0}.
{aⁿbⁿcⁿ} is not context-free by the pumping lemma for CFLs (3.6). So the family is not closed under ∩.

Complement fails by De Morgan. For any sets, L1 ∩ L2 = complement(complement L1 ∪ complement L2). If CFLs were closed under complement, both complements would be context-free, their union context-free by union closure, and the complement of that union context-free, making every intersection context-free. It is not. So complement closure fails.
Do not test complement on {aⁿbⁿ}: its complement is a CFL, so that proves nothing.

sections.h3: Decision properties that travel with this topic

blocks.text: A decision property is a yes/no question with an algorithm that always halts and answers correctly.

head: Question about a CFG G
Decidable?
Method
rows: simplify, then look for a usable A with A ⇒⁺ αAβ

blocks.text: Emptiness: mark every terminal, then every variable with a fully marked right side. L(G) is nonempty exactly when S ends up marked.
Finiteness: remove useless symbols, ε-rules and unit rules first (3.4). The language is infinite exactly when some usable variable can derive a string containing itself.
Equivalence of two CFGs and ambiguity of one grammar are undecidable; proofs belong to Unit 6. Emptiness of L(G1) ∩ L(G2) is also undecidable, though emptiness of each single L(Gi) is decidable.

spec.aria: Two overlapping ovals: L1 with ab, aabbc, abccc; L2 with bc, abbcc, aaabc; the overlap holds ε, abc, aabbcc, the language aⁿbⁿcⁿ, marked not context-free.

examples.question: L1 = {aⁿbⁿcᵐ : n, m ≥ 0} has grammar G1: S1 → AC, A → aAb, A → ε, C → cC, C → ε. L2 = {aᵐbⁿcⁿ : n, m ≥ 0} has grammar G2: S2 → DB, D → aD, D → ε, B → bBc, B → ε. (a) Write a grammar for L1 ∪ L2 and give its number of variables and productions. (b) Write a grammar for L1L2 and give its number of productions. (c) Find L1 ∩ L2 and count its strings of length at most 6.
steps: G1: variables S1, A, C (3); productions S1 → AC, A → aAb, A → ε, C → cC, C → ε (5). A builds aⁿbⁿ, C builds cᵐ.
G2: variables S2, D, B (3); productions S2 → DB, D → aD, D → ε, B → bBc, B → ε (5). D builds aᵐ, B builds bⁿcⁿ.
The variable names are already disjoint, so no renaming is needed.
(a) Union: new start S with S → S1, S → S2. Variables 3 + 3 + 1 = 7. Productions 5 + 5 + 2 = 12.
(b) Concatenation: new start S with S → S1S2. Variables 7. Productions 5 + 5 + 1 = 11.
(c) A string of L1 has n a's, n b's, m c's; a string of L2 has m a's, n b's, n c's. Both hold only when m = n, so L1 ∩ L2 = {aⁿbⁿcⁿ : n ≥ 0}.
By the pumping lemma this set is not context-free, so CFLs are not closed under intersection.
Lengths 3n ≤ 6: n = 0 gives ε, n = 1 gives abc, n = 2 gives aabbcc, n = 3 gives length 9. So 3 strings.
examples.answer: The union grammar has 7 variables and 12 productions, the concatenation grammar has 11 productions, and L1 ∩ L2 = {aⁿbⁿcⁿ : n ≥ 0}, which contains 3 strings of length at most 6 and is not context-free.

traps: Reading “CFL ∩ regular = CFL” as “CFL ∩ CFL = CFL”. The regular side lets one machine track both; two PDAs would need two stacks.
Testing complement on {aⁿbⁿ}: that complement is context-free. Use the De Morgan argument on L1 and L2.
Combining grammars without renaming variables: rules cross over and generate strings in neither language.
Writing the star rule as S → S1S1: that gives exactly two copies. Use S → SS1 and S → ε.
Emptiness of one CFL is decidable; emptiness of the intersection of two CFLs is not.

quiz.q: Name four operations under which context-free languages are closed.
quiz.a: Union, concatenation, Kleene star, reversal (also homomorphism and intersection with a regular set).

quiz.q: Name two operations under which context-free languages are not closed.
Why must the variable sets of two grammars be made disjoint before you combine them?
quiz.a: Each variable must mean one thing. If A means aAb in G1 and aA in G2, rules cross over and produce strings outside L1 ∪ L2.

quiz.q: G1: S1 → aS1b | ε and G2: S2 → cS2 | ε. Write a grammar for L1L2 and give its number of variables and productions.
quiz.a: S → S1S2 plus the four original rules: 5 productions. Variables S, S1, S2: 3 variables.

quiz.q: Use closure properties to show that L = {w in {a,b,c}* : w has equally many a, b and c} is not context-free.
quiz.a: a*b*c* is regular, and L ∩ a*b*c* = {aⁿbⁿcⁿ}, not a CFL (3.6). A CFL intersected with a regular set stays a CFL, so L cannot be a CFL.

quiz.q: Explain how closure under complement plus closure under union would force closure under intersection, and why that settles the complement question.
quiz.a: L1 ∩ L2 = complement(complement L1 ∪ complement L2). Complement and union closure would give intersection closure. Intersection is not closed, and union is, so complement must fail.

quiz.q: Is the complement of {aⁿbⁿ : n ≥ 0} over {a,b} context-free? Justify.
quiz.a: Yes. It is the union of strings containing ba, strings aⁱbʲ with i > j, and strings aⁱbʲ with i < j. Each is context-free, and union of CFLs is a CFL. So this example says nothing about non-closure.

quiz.q: A CFG G1 and a CFG G2 are given. Is the question "is L(G1) ∩ L(G2) empty?" decidable?
quiz.a: No. Emptiness of each single language is decidable, but emptiness of the intersection of two context-free languages is undecidable.

beyond: Not for the exam. Intersection with a regular set drives CFL-reachability, a static-analysis method that asks whether a value can flow from one program point to another by treating program edges as grammar rules and intersecting with a regular set of well-formed paths. Parser generators use the same split. Grammar-based verification of XML and configuration files layers regular constraints on tree structure.
